body: I should clarify that the old implementation behavior prior to the recent change was that a `dir=auto` element that contained no strong characters would fall back to `ltr`.
I would suggest we revert to the behavior it had for a very long time. The upside is not worth the downstream cost.

A little more history here:

In November 2010, `dir=auto` was added in fd6901dbbe7c178cdde54e53f4f8aae8e6c28393, fixing http://www.w3.org/Bugs/Public/show_bug.cgi?id=10808, with the behavior that `dir=auto` elements with no strong characters are `ltr`.

In April 2013, in work tied to https://www.w3.org/Bugs/Public/show_bug.cgi?id=17835, b00c2b0b092e7ceb1ecdb9c103010a6f1f961ba5 added the rule that `dir=auto` elements inherit parent directionality if they have no strong characters and are not a `<bdi>`.

In June 2013, also tied to https://www.w3.org/Bugs/Public/show_bug.cgi?id=17835, b967fb3c7e23d7aaf53b58e3b6e59216f8e3bc58 removed the exception for `<bdi>` that was added in April 2013.

In July 2013, fixing https://www.w3.org/Bugs/Public/show_bug.cgi?id=17835#c21, 773c6d1ba2d2028f88289ba945933592e40d4df2 changed the rule from being that elements inherit the parent directionality if they have no strong characters, to that they only inherit the parent directionality if they are empty (and nonempty elements with no strong characters are LTR).

In August 2014, without clear explanation, d2021df727adb22ee6d4c7e7968aa5abbd93a307 changed the rule from only empty element inheriting from the parent (and non-empty elements without strong characters being ltr) to instead being that any elements without strong characters inherit from the parent.  (This undid the July 2013 change, and went back to the June 2013 state.)

I believe the spec behavior for this case has not changed since then.

I should test which of the above behaviors existing implementations follow.
cc @aharon-lanin

There will certainly be cases where `dir=auto` containing no strongly directional characters results in broken display by applying either of the specific directions (either `ltr` or `rtl`). The bidi isolation of the element will help prevent broader spillover effects, but the element itself can still be broken.

My guess is that forcing `ltr` is wrong because RTL content authors would then have no control over the direction of `dir=auto` content. Many RTL language pages declare direction on e.g. the `html` element and don't repeated it internally. 


Note that I18N's staff contact has changed (@r12a is still around, but please copy... @xfq)

I tend to agree with @annevk 
But @jfkthame might have other opinions.

Note that the behavior it had "for a very long time" was because we didn't address bidirectionality thoroughly for a very long time.

There is also some history in the HTML Bidi requirements doc [at this location](https://www.w3.org/TR/html-bidi/#h.eeyazzsrd073)

Also, note that the [bug](https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=1521783) mentioned in the start of this issue has to do with how the Unicode Bidi Algorithm works with numbers (numbers are not strongly directional). 

If you have a negative number (`-1.7` say), the display of the minus sign will be incorrect if it is not prefixed with a character such as the ALM (U+061C) or LRM (U+200E). Some I18N libraries such as ICU4J, produce ALM while `Intl.NumberFormat` will produce LRM when formatting such a number. If no prefixing is done, the results can have the minus sign "swing around" to the other side depending on the direction. `dir=auto` isn't magic... sometimes UBA needs more help.

My first instinct was to feel that the "new" behavior (in the spec for the past decade, but not actually implemented in browsers until the recent Chrome change) would be preferable, but I'm not sure it's worth the potential compat issues of changing something that's been established on the web for so many years.

I don't believe there is any ideal algorithm or heuristic that can be relied on to automatically give the desired result in all cases; whatever we do, added "hints" in the form of bidi control characters and/or properties will sometimes be needed. Given this, stability should probably trump the possibly-marginal benefits of the change.

So +1 to @annevk, I think.

This is a complicated area.  The expected behaviour for numbers and punctuation varies according to what punctuation marks are involved, whether and what characters precede the expression, and what language this is. See https://r12a.github.io/scripts/arab/arb.html#expressions

For example, if this was a sentence capturing data related to 'Change in flow rate' (written in Arabic), and it was provided with the value written in memory as '100‐200' (ie. an increase) using ‐ U+2010 HYPHEN as the separator (which is appropriate), you'd expect to see '200-100' rendered in an Arabic sentence (but '100-200' in a Hebrew sentence).  Enter those values in the [JS Fiddle](https://jsfiddle.net/haxxmaxx/ehzm3bdq/13/) and Chrome shows '200-100' (indicating an increase), but Firefox applies LTR direction and so you get '100-200', which in a true RTL context would indicate a decrease rather than an increase.  (Note, that this behaviour is different from what you get when using - U+002D HYPHEN-MINUS.)

So that's at least one example that counters the one using the negative sign, but i expect that working out all the possible scenarios and effects is a little complicated, and i'm not sure what to recommend at the moment.  It seems as if Chrome's approach might possibly be safer when working with data being dropped into inline text, but that's just a hunch at the moment. 

On the other hand, if a telephone number or a MAC address string are dropped into an Arabic sentence, then applying LTR directionality would usually be recommended – you don't want the component parts moving around.  I don't know whether there's a one-size-fits-all answer to the use case described (which ignores metadata that comes with the data inserted, or an expectation of what type of data the insertion is (eg. a MAC address), that can be used to set the dir attribute on the inline element).

Not sure that helps us get closer to an answer, but it may hopefully advise a little caution in drawing conclusions here.

Here's a [quick test](https://w3c.github.io/i18n-tests/exploratory/vanilla/index.html?text=%3Cdiv%20dir%3D%22rtl%22%3E%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AA%D8%BA%D9%8A%D8%B1%20%D9%81%D9%8A%20%D9%85%D8%B9%D8%AF%D9%84%20%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AA%D8%AF%D9%81%D9%82%3A%20%3Cspan%20%20dir%3D%22auto%22%3E100%26%23x2010%3B200%3C%2Fspan%3E%3C%2Fdiv%3E&lang=ar&fontSize=36&width=500&height=500&a=&i=) to show the range example. It gives different results in Firefox and Chrome, but Chrome is the one that's correct this time.

So I wrote a [quick test for the inheritance cases](https://issues.chromium.org/u/1/issues/41494751#comment9) and it looks like the behavior prior to the recent Chromium change was the same in all engines:  `dir=auto` was LTR if there were no strong characters, and inheritance wasn't a thing.  Given that the discussion here doesn't have a clear conclusion that the new Chromium behavior is better, I'm going to revert Chromium back to the old behavior on that point.

Pulling up my comment from https://www.w3.org/Bugs/Public/show_bug.cgi?id=17835:

> The reason for [having all-neutral paragraphs resolve to LTR] is to keep the reordering results consistent with plaintext. In plaintext, a paragraph of neutral characters is ordered LTR.
>
> I don't mind defaulting to the inherited direction when the element is empty, if that makes for a better UI, but when it has neutral content, it should default to LTR regardless of the inherited direction.

Basically regardless of compatibility, I think reverting neutral sequences to LTR is the right answer.

@fantasai For otherwise RTL text, that breaks the directional run when it does not need to. Here's a quick-and-dirty example: >``` > البحرين مصر {{}} الكويت! >``` In the example, defaulting to LTR causes what is otherwise a unidirectional string to be bidirectional. This is visible in selection: ![image](https://github.com/whatwg/html/assets/69082/0094a761-24c2-4ddb-a636-c90b2e0980b3) [Try it](https://w3c.github.io/i18n-discuss/explainers/bidi-html-demo.html?text=\u0627\u0644\u0628\u062d\u0631\u064a\u0646%20\u0645\u0635\u0631%20%3Cspan%20dir=auto%3E{{}}%3C/span%3E%20\u0627\u0644\u0643\u0648\u064a\u062a!)
@aphillips That seems appropriate. It looks weird only because you chose a palindrome.

@fantasai I'm not explaining it well then. Replace the brackets with two other neutrals then. Let's says it's `.!`. The neutrals are reordered LTR even though there is no reason to. Now the selection looks like the following, with the `.` reordered on the left when there's no apparent reason for it to be: ![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/86111238-858f-4395-aca6-ca606e25a8c5) Now if we insert an RTL character (for `auto` see) we get selection that proceeds RTL because no LTR run is introduced by `auto`. The selection proceeds consistently RTL and the text continues to be ordered RTL all the way through. This is what an RTL speaker would expect, I think, based on looking at just the text alone: ![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a3f161af-eb83-42a0-9d11-ed246990cd19) ![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f5fc322a-14b2-453e-8120-ef834b41b4b3) Or weak sequences: ![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6b6bcd79-721d-4f01-826c-088ccf022095) My point is that the LTR default causes the `auto` span to introduce a reorder of the spanned text when none is called for by the text itself.

In our [2025-03-13](https://www.w3.org/2025/03/13-i18n-minutes.html#773d) teleconference, the I18N WG actioned me to reopen this issue. We think that defaulting `auto` to `ltr` is not the right behavior for elements that contain no strongly directional characters vs. using the established directional context.

We'd like to better understand HTML's reasoning behind this choice. Below we link a slightly improved example, similar to the one in my previous comment just above, showing text in-line (mid-string) vs. with dir=auto (end of each line)

[example](https://w3c.github.io/i18n-discuss/explainers/bidi-html-demo.html?text=\u0628%20%3Cspan%3E10-20%3C/span%3E%20\u0628%20%3Cspan%20dir=auto%3E10-20%3C/span%3E%3Cbr%3E\u0628%20%3Cspan%3E10!%3C/span%3E%20\u0628%20%3Cspan%20dir=auto%3E10!%3C/span%3E)

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d6c36594-6707-4d65-90a6-b2581fe757f7)

\* Note that there is some complexity wrt the handling of numbers in Hebrew and Persian

At this point webcompat is rather important reasoning for the current spec, I think. Last year there was great amount of work to have better interoperability https://wpt.fyi/results/html/dom/elements/global-attributes?label=master&label=experimental&aligned&view=interop&q=label%3Ainterop-2024-dir between browsers as part of interop-2024.
So, in case it is agreed that defaulting auto to ltr isn't the right model, before changing the behavior of the spec and all the implementations someone should collect data about how many sites might be broken if the behavior was changed.

It may be useful to expound a little on Addison's example. Here is the example of a range, 10-20. (This also applies to expressions.) (The markup is forced to be LTR override, for readability.) In this diagram i put a label A against the behaviour you would expect for Arabic by default. The range naturally flows from right to left if there's no markup involved. As you can see, if dir=auto is applied around the range then the result B is now broken, due to the application of the LTR direction. (Same principle applies to the 10! example above.) So it's likely that defaulting to LTR is likely to _break_ many sites where text is injected into the HTML; treating the range as part of the surrounding text, without imposing LTR, is likely to actually _fix_ those sites, rather than break them. Things are a little more complicated than this, as alluded to in my earlier post, since Hebrew ranges do indeed flow from left to right, though that should just be handled by the bidi algorithm - no need to apply LTR markup. (Persian is a special case because it also flows LTR.). But basically, for Arabic text, the default LTR application is actually breaking the expected behaviour.

On the other hand, if the injected `dir=auto` span were a phone number like `+1 (800) 555-1212`, I think the expectation for most (all?) languages would be that it should be displayed fully LTR. That's what we currently see in browsers, as a result of the default-LTR behavior when no strong characters are present; but if I understand correctly, the suggested change would break such examples.

My current feeling is that neither option is universally better. I think that to justify a _breaking change_ to longstanding interoperable¹ behavior, it would have to meet a pretty high bar of greater correctness and usefulness, and I don't see that here.

¹ Modulo the brief period when Blink tried changing behavior, which led to this whole discussion.

Yes, the telephone number and things like MAC addresses are (incidentally) helped by `auto` producing LTR direction, but (and we discussed this in the i18n call, though i didn't write about it here until now) i see these as special cases.  Ideally, it would either be known that you are receiving this particular type of text which you know runs LTR and which you can mark up as such, or when these strings are inserted there would be some metadata to indicate that the direction should be set to LTR.  In other words, we shouldn't really be dumping telephone numbers into anodyne elements with dir set to `auto`. Of course, this is only an issue if you are injecting text into content — if you're writing the content (or if you know what type of data you are receiving), you should mark up the direction as part of that process, and the direction in the receiving container should just be set to LTR, and not auto.

There will probably be cases where the developer has not considered this, and (unless some AI is applied to guess at what it is we are dealing with) everything gets lumped under `auto`.  In that case we need to choose whether, on the whole, we want ranges and expressions, and negative numbers (per the original bug report) to look correct, or telephone numbers. In principle, i would think that the former should automatically look correct, and that the latter should be handled with a little more care.  I suppose it may depend on the level of breakage that is actually incurred for things like telephone numbers compared to ranges, but even so, getting negative numbers right seems pretty fundamental.  Also, my experience with people using RTL scripts is that they expect things like telephone numbers to be messed up anyway, due to long experience, and just deal with it.

As you say, it's not clear cut, but it worries me more that negative numbers and expressions are being systematically mishandled than that telephone numbers are automatically correct.

I hope it's okay that I, a user in an RTL-speaking country, say what would IMO be the most useful behavior for `dir="auto"`: 1. If there's any strongly-directional character in the contents (ignoring bidi-isolated elements or text), use the direction of the first one. This matches current behavior in all browsers AFAIK. 2. Else, if there's any weakly-directional character (like digits) (ignoring bidi-isolated elements or text), use the direction of the first one. This makes things like phone numbers and negative numbers appear correctly. 3. Else, if there are bidi-isolated child elements or text (`` or `dir=*` or others like that) which have an explicit direction *or* have determined their direction using rule 1, use the computed direction of the first such element. **This rule is important.** More on this below. 4. Else, repeat rule 3 but include elements which have determined their direction using rule 2. 5. Else, inherit the direction of the parent. We're pretty much left with only punctuation marks, so they should match surrounding text. 6. Dealing with a real edge case here, but if it's the root element and there's no parent to inherit from - either default to LTR or default to the direction of the browser's UI (which would likely match the direction of operating system). To me, this is how I expect automatic direction to behave. I can't think of a counter-example where the result would be the opposite of what anyone intended. I'm open to being proven wrong. Edit: after more thoroughly reading the discussion above, it seems number ranges within Arabic text should be RTL, unlike Hebrew where they're LTR. Call me crazy, but number ranges should not be in a `dir="auto"` element isolated from the rest of the text. And besides, my suggested behavior would match legacy behavior in this case anyway! ---- So, rule 3. What am I on about? Here's an example. Consider this Markdown: ``` > מילה > > או שתיים ``` In an open forum (like this comments section) each paragraph typically gets the `dir="auto"` tag, resulting in: ```html

מילה

או שתיים

``` > מילה > > או שתיים But the blockquote itself is going the wrong way! Even if its styling used `border-inline-start` instead of `border-left`, without rule 3 there would be no possible way to make the `
` detect the direction of the text within it. If rule 3 is applied, then the following would create a RTL blockquote with two RTL paragraphs: ```html

מילה

או שתיים

``` Without rule 3, a web developer has no reasonable way to make the blockquote go in the right direction. Fiddle: https://jsfiddle.net/6njyos80/1/ Edit: if anyone doesn't want to click that link, the fiddle HTML is: ```html With auto:

מילה

או שתיים

Bad output:

מילה

או שתיים

Desired output:

מילה

או שתיים

``` and the CSS: ```css blockquote { padding: 0 1em; border-inline-start: .25em solid grey; } ``` Edit: tweaked the rules to be more self-consistent. See edit history of this comment if you're interested.
